extracted.intended_audience: young men and local political operatives seeking practical advice on succeeding as Tammany Hall district leaders (early 20th‑century New York City)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, prescriptive advice and tactics for becoming and remaining a successful Tammany Hall politician and district leader in New York City — covering graft, patronage, organization, constituent service, and campaign techniques. The guidance is rooted in grassroots, machine‑style urban politics of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish honest graft from dishonest graft
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an 'honest graft' and a 'dishonest graft' — the former is taking advantage of lawful opportunities (e.g., buying land before public improvements) while the latter is blackmail, dealing with gamblers, saloonkeepers, disorderly people, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: buying land near a planned park or bridge, buying city‑sold paving stones and reselling; avoid outright theft, blackmail, and collusion with criminal enterprises. Emphasize foresight and legal means: 'I seen my opportunities and I took 'em.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert for and seize opportunities (foresight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political success depends on spotting opportunities (public improvements, sales of city materials, appointments) and acting quickly to profit or to strengthen position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical examples given (land for parks, swamp for park completion, repaving granite blocks). The counsel is continuous vigilance and prompt action whenever an opening presents itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get a following — marketable goods (votes) matter
rubrics_metrics.description: To enter politics, bring a 'marketable commodity' — even one vote — then expand it into a following that you can offer party leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start small: recruit neighbors, house by house; form associations (e.g., 'George Washington Plunkitt Association'); a following gains you attention, nominations, and bargaining power with leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical experience over book learning or oratory
rubrics_metrics.description: Colleges, books, and oratorical skill are largely useless in machine politics; what counts is practical street work and the ability to keep your tongue still when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work at district headquarters, hustle on election day, do the grunt work rather than relying on speeches or academic credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin political apprenticeship early
rubrics_metrics.description: Start helping out in politics before you can vote — work polls, help get voters out, serve at district headquarters — to learn the 'a, b, c of politics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early involvement produces trained operatives; those who begin young are likelier to become lasting statesmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use patronage / spoils to reward workers
rubrics_metrics.description: When in power, place party workers in offices and give them opportunities; patronage preserves party loyalty and yields votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raise salaries for clerks to win votes; prefer party workers 'if they are fitted to perform the duties of the office.' Position distribution is a deliberate means to hold power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous, all‑year‑round organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Politics is not episodic; maintain organization and activity through the year — never close your headquarters and always be ready to mobilize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions include frequent meetings of captains, maintaining records of voters, and constant outreach to constituents; a leader's HQ should be 'never closed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct, personal constituent service (reach hearts, not heads)
rubrics_metrics.description: Win votes through material help and visible presence: visiting courts, bailing out constituents, attending funerals/weddings, providing relief, and giving gifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and a day schedule show minute‑by‑minute constituent service: rescuing fire victims, paying rents, securing jobs, attending social events — all aimed at building gratitude and loyalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study human nature and act accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: To hold a district, understand the desires, needs, and emotions of constituents and act in ways that appeal to them rather than relying on abstract principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor appeals to sympathy and immediate needs; prioritize practical benefits and favors over ideology or policy lectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep omnipresence and visibility in the community
rubrics_metrics.description: Be known to everyone in the district; attend public and private events conspicuously so constituents associate you with help and presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appear at church/synagogue services, fairs, balls, and civic events; lead dances, buy tickets, and be seen distributing assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize and train local captains and agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Use election district captains to maintain voter lists, report attitudes, identify needs, and execute instructions; centralized coordination by the leader is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold regular meetings, collect lists, assign tasks (look for 'drunks and disorderlies' as vote‑getters), and keep notes for targeted outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit social and cultural rituals to gain advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Winning ethnic and neighborhood blocs requires participating in and investing in their rituals — christenings, weddings, funerals, confirmations — and being generous at these moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hire agents to monitor civil marriage bureaus, send presents quickly, pay funeral expenses, and otherwise be first and most generous to ingratiate yourself with communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage public entertainments and large‑scale events
rubrics_metrics.description: Outings, beefsteak dinners, balls, and festivals foster group loyalty and publicize a leader's generosity and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify attendance and consumption as bragging rights; use events to bind constituents (men's and women's outings, winter balls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be competitive and opportunistic in intra‑machine contests
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proactive tactics (spies, hiring reporters, preemptive purchases or services) to beat rival leaders in showing up first and providing more to constituents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hiring men at the marriage bureau, booking all carriages for a funeral, bribing jewelers for information — ethically dubious but effective within the machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize local practical issues over abstract national debates
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus campaign messages and platform items on issues that excite the masses (e.g., patronage, jobs) rather than abstruse topics people don't care about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate simple, attention‑grabbing planks (the text suggests a platform attacking civil service reform) and avoid lengthy doctrinal disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use salary increases as vote‑getting measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Raising salaries of department clerks and other officeholders converts recipients into loyal voters — 'Tammany gains ten votes for every one it lost by salary raisin'.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement modest raises broadly to build sympathy and electoral support among salaried workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect and cultivate local economic interests (home industries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Support and patronize local businesses and industries to demonstrate protection of 'home industries' and to gain political capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid patronizing outside businesses when local patronage can be claimed for political advantage; use procurement and events to reward local vendors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a visible record of daily activity (diary‑like accountability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A leader's routine, documented and reported, reinforces image of constant service and hard work — from early morning calls to late‑night social visits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicize or at least keep internal records of interventions (bails, charities, court attendances) to show usefulness and dedication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit government projects and legislation to benefit your district
rubrics_metrics.description: Use knowledge of pending public works and legislative actions to acquire land, jobs, or contracts that can be turned into resources for supporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include buying land needed for parks or bridge approaches, and participating in distribution of contracts or materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reformist pretensions — learn politics as a profession
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform movements are temporary; successful leaders are political professionals trained over years and dedicated full‑time to the craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect business men or amateur reformers to sustain political change; training and specialization matter.
